subtopicTitle: Rule of Zero — prefer compiler-generated specials

cards.front: What is the C++ "Rule of Zero"?
cards.back: It states that if a class does not manage any resources (e.g., raw pointers, file handles, network sockets), then it should not declare *any* user-defined special member functions.

cards.front: What is the primary advantage of adhering to the C++ Rule of Zero?
cards.back: It simplifies class design by allowing the compiler to generate all special member functions (constructor, destructor, copy/move operations) correctly, avoiding the complexities and common errors associated with manual resource management and the Rule of Three/Five/Six.

cards.front: List all the special member functions that the C++ compiler will implicitly generate if they are not user-declared.
cards.back: Default constructor, destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment operator, move constructor, move assignment operator.

cards.front: According to the Rule of Zero, how should a C++ class manage dynamic memory or other resources?
cards.back: A class should *delegate* resource management to dedicated resource-managing classes (e.g., `std::unique_ptr`, `std::shared_ptr`, `std::vector`, `std::string`, `std::fstream`). The class itself should only contain these resource-managing objects, not raw resources.

cards.front: Explain the relationship between the Rule of Zero and the Rule of Three/Five/Six.
cards.back: The Rule of Three/Five/Six states that if you define *any* of the special member functions (destructor, copy ctor/assign, move ctor/assign) manually, you likely need to define *all* of them. The Rule of Zero provides a simpler alternative: by *not* managing resources directly, you don't need to define *any* of them, thus completely sidestepping the complexities of the Rule of Three/Five/Six.

cards.front: For the class `struct Vec2 { double x, y; };`, does the Rule of Zero suggest defining any special member functions? Explain.
cards.back: No. `Vec2` only contains built-in types (`double`), which do not manage any resources. The compiler-generated default constructor, destructor, copy/move constructors, and copy/move assignment operators will all perform the correct member-wise operations.
